title: What ESD-Safe Tweezers Are
description: ESD-safe tweezers are precision tweezers with a dissipative coating or material that drains static instead of delivering it to the part — for handling motherboard jumpers, M.2 thermal pads, tiny screws, and SMD components. Fingers are too big and too charged for this work; regular steel tweezers can zap a part. The black ESD coating is the visual tell.

demo.program:
print("ESD tweezers: dissipative coating drains static (no zap on touch).")
print("Jobs: jumpers, M.2 pads, tiny screws, SMD parts.")
print("Fingers: too big + too charged. Regular tweezers: can zap.")
print("Black coating = the visual tell.")

t: How the ESD Coating Protects Parts
title: How the ESD Coating Protects Parts
description: The coating (usually epoxy with conductive filler) gives the tweezer a surface resistivity in the dissipative range — charge flows away slowly instead of arcing. The tweezers are part of the grounded workstation: used on the mat, often with the wrist strap on, they extend your ESD-safe handling to parts your fingers cannot safely touch. Coating worn through to bare metal at the tips is normal; the handles must stay coated.

demo.program:
print("Dissipative coating: charge drains slowly, never arcs.")
print("Workstation rule: tweezers ON the mat, strap ON the wrist.")
print("Tip wear to metal: normal. Handle coating worn: replace.")
print("They extend ESD-safe handling past what fingers can do.")

t: Tip Types: Pointed, Flat, Curved, and Reverse-Action
title: Tip Types: Pointed, Flat, Curved, and Reverse-Action
description: Pointed tips: jumpers, SMD parts, precision placement. Flat/blunt tips: thermal pads, stickers, larger parts — more grip area. Curved tips: reaching around components. Reverse-action (squeeze to open): hold parts without constant pressure — the tweezer grips at rest, ideal for placing many identical parts. One pointed plus one flat covers most PC work.

print("pointed : jumpers, SMD, precision. flat: pads, stickers, grip area.")
print("curved  : reach around parts. reverse-action: grips at rest (no fatigue).")
print("PC kit: one pointed + one flat covers ~everything.")

t: Sizing and Grip: What Fits Hands and Work
title: Sizing and Grip: What Fits Hands and Work
description: Standard ESD tweezers run 4.5-5 inches — long enough for case interiors, short enough for control. The grip should be light: death-gripping launches tiny parts across the room. Look for alignment that meets perfectly at the tips (test on a hair) and a tension that holds without effort. Cheap tweezers with misaligned tips are worse than fingers.

print("Test: tips meet perfectly (try a hair). Misaligned = worse than fingers.")
print("Tension: holds without effort. Your hand shouldn't work to keep grip.")

t: Use Case: Motherboard Jumpers and Front-Panel Pins
title: Use Case: Motherboard Jumpers and Front-Panel Pins
description: Jumpers are the tweezer's signature PC job: pointed tips place and remove jumper caps on headers your fingers cannot fit between. Grip the cap's sides (not top), lift straight, place straight — angled force bends pins. For front-panel connectors, tweezers seat the tiny blocks onto header pins precisely. The right tool turns a frustrating job into a precise one.

print("Front-panel blocks: tweezers seat precisely on header pins.")
print("Fingers can't fit; tweezers make it precise instead of frustrating.")

t: Use Case: M.2 Thermal Pads and Small Adhesives
title: Use Case: M.2 Thermal Pads and Small Adhesives
description: M.2 thermal pads are sticky, thin, and exactly fingertip-resistant — flat-tip tweezers peel the backing, position the pad, and press it down without fingerprints (skin oil hurts thermal transfer). Same for chipset pads and adhesive cable mounts. The rule: anything sticky or thermal gets tweezers, because fingers contaminate what tweezers place cleanly.

print("Thermal pads: peel backing, position, press - NO fingerprints (oil hurts transfer).")
print("Sticky/adhesive parts: tweezers place cleanly, fingers contaminate.")
print("Rule: sticky or thermal = tweezers, always.")

t: Use Case: Retrieving and Placing Tiny Screws
title: Use Case: Retrieving and Placing Tiny Screws
description: Tweezers place M.2 screws into standoffs your fingers cannot reach, and retrieve screws the pickup magnet cannot (brass, aluminum, plastic). Technique: grip the screw's threads lightly near the head, guide don't push, and release over the hole — let gravity seat it, then drive. Dropped screws get tweezed from flat surfaces faster than any magnet.

print("Non-ferrous retrieval (brass/alu/plastic): tweezers beat magnets.")
print("Flat-surface pickup: tweezers faster than any magnet sweep.")

t: Technique: The Light Touch and the Rest Position
title: Technique: The Light Touch and the Rest Position
description: The technique: hold tweezers like a pen (not a fist), grip with the minimum force that holds, and move with the wrist braced on the bench or case edge — braced hands do not shake. Rest the tweezers on the mat (not the board) between uses. Shaky hands are usually unbraced hands; brace first, then blame caffeine.

print("Rest on MAT between uses (never on the board).")
print("Shaky = unbraced. Brace first, blame caffeine second.")

title: Maintenance: Cleaning Tips and Recoating
description: Wipe tips with IPA after adhesive work — sticky buildup ruins precision. Check tip alignment monthly: bent tips get carefully rebent or the tweezer retires. The ESD coating cannot be recoated at home; when handles wear to bare metal over large areas, replace the tweezer — its protection is gone. Tips are consumable-adjacent; handles are the investment.

print("Monthly: alignment check (bent -> rebend carefully or retire).")
print("Handle coating worn large: REPLACE (protection gone, can't recoat at home).")

t: ESD Tweezers vs Fingers vs Pliers
title: ESD Tweezers vs Fingers vs Pliers
description: Tweezers: precise, ESD-safe, for small parts — the PC choice. Fingers: too big, too oily, too charged for jumpers and pads. Pliers: too strong, crush small parts, no ESD safety — for screws and standoffs, never for jumpers. The hierarchy is clear: if it is small and electronic, it gets tweezers.

print("pliers  : strong, crush, no ESD. Screws/standoffs only, never jumpers.")

title: Buying Guide: What to Check
description: Check: tip alignment (must meet perfectly), ESD marking (look for the ESD-safe symbol and dissipative spec), comfortable light tension, and a protective tip cover or case. Expect 8-15 dollars for a good pair; the 3-dollar pairs have misaligned tips and mystery coating. Buy pointed first, flat second — that order matches PC need frequency.

t: Advanced: SMD Rework and Fine-Pitch Handling
title: Advanced: SMD Rework and Fine-Pitch Handling
description: For SMD rework (replacing capacitors, BIOS chips), curved fine tips plus a magnifier handle parts down to 0402 size — tweezers hold the part while the iron tacks one side, then the other. Keep a dedicated ultra-fine pair for rework; daily PC tweezers are too blunt. Fine-pitch work is where tweezer quality shows: cheap tips flex and drop the part.

title: Storage: Tip Protection Discipline
description: Tips bend in drawers — store tweezers in their covers, in a stand, or in the bench station's tool slot, tips up or protected. Never toss them loose with screwdrivers. A bent tip is a retired tweezer for precision work; the discipline of putting them away is what keeps precision precise.

t: Common Mistakes: Magnetizing, Over-Gripping, Wrong Tips
title: Common Mistakes: Magnetizing, Over-Gripping, Wrong Tips
description: Mistakes: using magnetic tweezers near sensitive parts (magnetized tips attract filings into boards), death-gripping (launches parts), pointed tips for pads (pierces them), and using tweezers as pry bars (bends tips). Each has the same fix: the right tip, the right force, the right job. Tweezers are precise instruments, not tiny pliers.

print("Pointed on pads: pierces. Tweezers as pry bars: bends tips.")
print("Fix: right tip + right force + right job. Instruments, not tiny pliers.")
